title: The Toronto home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Toronto: what audits find in the city's brick semis and post-war bungalows, the rebates that stack (HRSP + HELP + $600 assessment rebate), and every registered auditor serving the city.
intro: Toronto is the best-funded place in Canada to fix a house right now: provincial rebates, the City's own low-interest HELP loans, and a $600 assessment rebate stack on the same project. It's also a city of old, leaky housing — which is exactly why the money exists.
housingStock: The classic Toronto house is a pre-war brick semi or Victorian rowhouse — solid masonry walls with no cavity to insulate, original attics, and air leakage everywhere. Ring around that core and you hit the post-war bungalows and side-splits of Scarborough, North York, and Etobicoke: empty 2×4 walls, R-10 attics, bare-concrete basements. Both profiles reward an audit-first approach, because the fixes differ completely — solid brick needs an interior or exterior insulation strategy, while post-war frame walls can often be drilled and filled.
commonFindings: Attic bypasses around chimneys and pot lights driving ice dams on brick semis
Knob-and-tube remnants in pre-1950 homes that block insulation work until an electrician signs off
Uninsulated solid-brick walls misdiagnosed as 'needs new windows'
Bare foundation walls in post-war bungalows losing 20%+ of the home's heat
Vermiculite in mid-century attics — sample before touching
programAngle: Toronto homeowners uniquely stack three layers: Home Renovation Savings (insulation up to $7,700, heat pumps up to $12,000, the $600 assessment rebate), the City's HELP program (loans to $125,000 at posted rates, most projects requiring the same EnerGuide assessment), and for CMHC-insured recent buyers, the 25% Eco Improvement premium refund. One assessment unlocks all three — which is why booking it is step one, not step five.

faq.q: Is an energy audit worth it on a 100-year-old Toronto semi?
faq.a: Old solid-brick homes benefit most: the audit distinguishes the fixes that work on masonry (air sealing, attic, basement, interior wall strategies) from the ones that don't, and its blower door number is usually dramatic enough to reorder your whole renovation plan.

faq.q: Do Toronto condos qualify?
faq.a: EnerGuide assessments and most rebates target houses and towns with their own envelope. In a condo, the corporation owns the envelope — your levers are in-suite sealing, and pushing the board toward a building-level audit.

title: The Ottawa home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Ottawa: cold-climate priorities for the capital's 1960s–80s housing stock, HRSP rebates, and registered energy advisors serving Ottawa and the valley.
intro: Ottawa winters are the coldest of any large Ontario city, which changes the math: every envelope upgrade pays back faster here, and undersized or oversized heat pumps get found out in the first cold snap.
housingStock: Ottawa grew fastest in the 1960s–80s, so the dominant profile is the suburban split and two-storey with R-8 to R-12 walls, R-20 attics, and original ductwork — plus older stock in Centretown, the Glebe, and Vanier, and rural properties on oil or propane in the surrounding townships. Electric baseboard is common in 1970s builds, making Ottawa prime heat-pump conversion territory — with the caveat that units must be sized for genuine -25°C performance, not brochure numbers.
commonFindings: Attics at half the insulation the climate calls for — the region's most reliable payback
Rim-joist leakage that makes split-level lower floors uncomfortable all winter
Electric baseboard homes paying 40–60% more for heat than a cold-climate heat pump would
Oil-heated rural homes with the fastest fuel-switch paybacks in the province
Ice damming on low-slope additions from warm-air bypasses
programAngle: Home Renovation Savings applies across Ottawa: the assessment path pays $600 toward your audits and up to $7,700 for insulation, and the no-assessment stream covers cold-climate heat pumps up to $12,000. For baseboard-heated homes, pairing the audit's CSA F280 heat-loss calculation with the heat pump rebate is the single highest-value move in the city.

faq.q: Do heat pumps actually work in Ottawa winters?
faq.a: Modern cold-climate units are rated to -25°C and beyond and heat Ottawa homes through almost every hour of the year — the failures you hear about are sizing failures. That's what the room-by-room heat-loss calculation prevents; get it before any quote.

faq.q: What should rural Ottawa-area homeowners do first?
faq.a: If you heat with oil or propane, the audit plus a heat-pump conversion usually beats every other investment — and the assessment documents the before/after that resale buyers increasingly ask for.

title: The Hamilton home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Hamilton: century brick, post-war steel-town stock, escarpment microclimates, HRSP rebates, and the registered auditors serving Hamilton, Ancaster, and Dundas.
intro: Hamilton's housing tells the city's story: century brick downtown, dense post-war neighbourhoods built for steelworkers, and newer suburbs climbing the escarpment. Each era fails differently — and the audit tells you which failure you own.
housingStock: Lower Hamilton runs to pre-war brick with empty or minimal wall insulation and original attics. The east end and Mountain filled in through the 1950s–70s with bungalows and back-splits — thin batts, R-10 to R-20 attics, unfinished basements. Ancaster, Dundas, and Waterdown add 1980s–2000s stock where ventilation and duct balance, not insulation depth, are the usual complaints. Lake and escarpment effects mean wind-driven leakage matters more here than the thermometer alone suggests.
commonFindings: Empty brick-veneer wall cavities in pre-1960 homes — drill-and-fill candidates
Attic top-ups from R-15 to R-60 as the city's most consistent payback
Basement moisture that must be addressed before insulation in the older lower city
Wind-exposed escarpment homes where air sealing outperforms its usual returns
Aging mid-efficiency furnaces due for the heat-pump-or-hybrid decision
programAngle: Hamilton is one of Ontario's better-supplied audit markets: Green Venture, the local non-profit service organization, works alongside province-wide firms — comparing a community quote against a commercial one is realistic here. Home Renovation Savings covers the standard stack: $600 assessment rebate, insulation to $7,700, heat pumps to $12,000.

faq.q: My Hamilton house is brick — can the walls even be insulated?
faq.a: Depends which brick: brick veneer over frame usually has a cavity that can be dense-packed; solid double-brick can't be filled and needs interior or exterior strategies. The audit's thermal scan tells you which you own before you spend a dollar.

faq.q: Who does audits in Hamilton?
faq.a: Green Venture (the Green Communities Canada member for Hamilton–Halton–Niagara) plus province-wide organizations like The Energuy and AmeriSpec. Every provider we list is an NRCan-licensed service organization.

title: The Mississauga home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Mississauga: what audits find in 1970s–90s subdivisions, HRSP rebates, and registered energy advisors serving Mississauga and south Peel.
intro: Mississauga was built in a hurry — most of it between 1970 and 2000 — and the shortcuts of fast subdivision construction are exactly what an audit is built to find.
housingStock: The city's core profile is the 1970s–90s two-storey: R-12-ish walls, R-20 to R-32 attics, builder-grade ductwork, and the infamous room over the garage. Older pockets in Port Credit, Streetsville, and Cooksville add post-war bungalows, while newer infill runs tighter but often under-ventilated. Nearly everything is gas-heated, which makes the heat-pump question a comfort-and-cooling decision as much as a bills one.
commonFindings: Cold rooms over garages from missed floor insulation and duct runs through unconditioned space
Second floors that roast in July — attic heat load plus leaky duct runs
Attic top-ups that still clear the bar at today's install prices
Poly-era homes with condensation issues traced to ventilation, not windows
Oversized builder furnaces short-cycling toward early failure
programAngle: The Home Renovation Savings assessment path fits Mississauga's profile: two or more upgrades (typically attic + air sealing, or insulation + windows) unlock the $600 assessment rebate plus up to $7,700 in insulation support. Duct testing is the add-on to request by name here — it explains most of the city's comfort complaints.

faq.q: Why is the room over my garage always cold?
faq.a: Because its floor faces unheated space and its ducts run through the same cold zone; builders routinely under-insulated both. The fix ladder runs duct sealing → floor insulation → a ductless head if needed — the audit's thermal scan shows which step yours needs.

faq.q: Is a heat pump worth it in a gas-heated Mississauga home?
faq.a: On pure bills, modest at current gas prices; as an AC-replacement decision, strong. When your air conditioner dies, the incremental cost of a heat pump over a new AC — minus up to $12,000 in rebates — usually makes it the obvious replacement.

title: The Brampton home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Brampton: newer stock, bigger homes, multigenerational households — what audits find, HRSP rebates, and registered advisors serving Brampton.
intro: Brampton's housing is newer and larger than most of the GTA — which means fewer empty walls, but bigger heating bills per household and comfort problems that scale with square footage.
housingStock: Most of Brampton went up after 1980, much of it after 2000: code-insulated walls, R-32+ attics, and two-storey layouts that concentrate problems upstairs. Large homes and multigenerational households push consumption up even when the envelope is decent — basement apartments and finished lower levels add their own comfort and ventilation questions. The audit's job here is less 'find the missing insulation' and more 'balance, size, and optimize.'
commonFindings: Unbalanced ductwork leaving second floors hot in summer, cold in winter
Finished basements insulated behind the drywall — or not — with no way to tell without a thermal scan
Ventilation shortfalls in tighter 2000s homes running high occupancy
Oversized furnaces and ACs cycling hard in large builds
Attic top-ups still worthwhile in pre-2010 sections
programAngle: The no-assessment stream fits many Brampton situations — heat pumps to $12,000 and attic insulation to $1,250 without the two-upgrade requirement — while larger retrofit plans (insulation + windows on bigger homes) justify the assessment path and its $600 rebate. For homes with basement units, the audit also documents ventilation and safety details that matter for legal second suites.

faq.q: Our house is only 15 years old — what would an audit even find?
faq.a: Typically: duct imbalance, a missed insulation bay or two, ventilation running below occupancy needs, and oversized equipment. Newer-home audits are optimization audits — smaller fixes, but cheap ones with quick paybacks, plus proper sizing for your eventual heat pump.

faq.q: Does a basement apartment change the audit?
faq.a: It changes what to ask for: ventilation assessment and combustion safety matter more with more occupants and closed-off zones, and the audit's documentation helps with second-unit compliance conversations.

title: The York Region home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Vaughan, Markham, Richmond Hill, Newmarket, and Aurora: what audits find across York Region's mixed stock, HRSP rebates, and the region's registered advisors.
intro: York Region runs the full spectrum — from Newmarket's older main-street homes to Markham's 2000s subdivisions — and it happens to host several of Canada's largest audit organizations. Getting two quotes here is easy; knowing what to ask them for is what this guide is for.
housingStock: Vaughan and Markham are dominated by 1980s–2010s two-storeys: poly vapour barriers, decent nominal insulation, builder ductwork, and ventilation as the sleeper issue. Richmond Hill, Aurora, and Newmarket mix in 1960s–70s splits and older village cores with emptier walls and thinner attics. Estate lots north of Major Mackenzie add large propane- and oil-heated properties where fuel-switch economics rival anything in the province.
commonFindings: Duct balance and bonus-room comfort failures in the newer two-storey stock
Condensation and stale air in tight-but-unventilated 1990s homes
Thin attics and rim-joist leakage in the older splits
Propane/oil estate homes with dramatic heat-pump conversion math
Finished basements hiding uninsulated foundation walls
programAngle: Several of the province's highest-volume service organizations are headquartered in York Region, so quote comparison is practical. Home Renovation Savings applies region-wide — $600 assessment rebate on the two-upgrade path, heat pumps to $12,000 — and rural properties on oil should price the switch even without a rebate deadline pushing them.

faq.q: Which audit company should I pick in York Region?
faq.a: Compare at least two — a community organization like Windfall against a volume provider — and judge on what they'll measure: confirm thermal imaging is included, and ask for duct testing if comfort is your complaint. Every listing on this site is NRCan-licensed; check their Google and HomeStars reviews from their profiles.

faq.q: We're on propane north of the city — priorities?
faq.a: Get the audit's heat-loss calculation and price a cold-climate heat pump conversion immediately; propane heating costs typically make the payback the fastest of any fuel, with or without rebates.

title: The Kitchener–Waterloo & Cambridge home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Waterloo Region: century homes, post-war stock and student rentals, Reep Green Solutions and other registered advisors, plus the HRSP rebate math.
intro: Waterloo Region pairs one of Ontario's oldest community-energy non-profits with a housing mix that runs from 1880s century homes to last decade's tech-boom builds. It's a place where the audit-first habit is genuinely local culture.
housingStock: Kitchener's core and Cambridge's Galt are rich in century homes — balloon framing, empty walls, stone foundations. Around them: broad rings of 1950s–70s bungalows and splits, student-rental conversions near the universities with deferred-maintenance envelopes, and newer suburbs in Waterloo and Breslau. The region's freeze-thaw winters make ice-dam diagnostics a staple of local audits.
commonFindings: Century-home leakage numbers that reorder the whole renovation plan
Stone foundations needing moisture strategy before insulation
Student rentals with the region's worst bills-per-square-foot — and cheapest fixes
Post-war attics at R-10 waiting for the region's most reliable payback
Ice dams from attic bypasses in snow-belt winters
programAngle: Reep Green Solutions has been delivering evaluations here since the 1990s alongside province-wide providers, and Home Renovation Savings applies as everywhere: $600 assessment rebate on the two-upgrade path, insulation to $7,700. Landlords: the assessment documents upgrades that increasingly matter to tenants comparing utility-included rents.

faq.q: Is an audit worth it on a century home in Kitchener?
faq.a: It's most valuable there: the blower door and thermal scan establish whether air sealing, attic, and basement work (the usual winners) can transform the house before you consider expensive wall strategies — and which walls even have cavities to fill.

faq.q: Who does audits in Waterloo Region?
faq.a: Reep Green Solutions is the community non-profit; The Energuy and AmeriSpec cover the region commercially. All are NRCan-licensed — compare a quote from each column.

title: The London home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in London, Ontario — neighbourhood by neighbourhood: Oakridge, Masonville, Sunningdale, Old North, Byron and more, with era-matched findings, HRSP rebates, and the city's registered energy advisors.
intro: London's snow-belt winters and older-than-average housing stock make it one of the highest-return audit cities in southwestern Ontario — the gap between a leaky house and a sealed one shows up hard on Forest City gas bills.
housingStock: Old North, Old East, and Wortley Village hold London's century stock — yellow-brick homes with empty walls and original attics. The post-war expansion filled Byron, Oakridge, and the east end with 1950s–70s bungalows and ranches: thin batts, bare basements, aging mid-efficiency furnaces. Lake-effect snow loads make attic bypasses especially visible here — ice dams are a London specialty.
commonFindings: Ice dams tracing back to attic air leaks rather than 'bad shingles'
Yellow-brick century homes where the thermal scan decides the wall strategy
R-10 post-war attics — the city's most consistent payback
Uninsulated basements in homes now finishing lower levels
Furnaces past 20 years facing the hybrid-or-heat-pump decision
programAngle: Home Renovation Savings runs the standard stack — $600 toward assessments, insulation to $7,700, windows at $100 per opening on the two-upgrade path. London's freeze-thaw pattern makes the air-sealing + attic combination the classic qualifying pair, usually fully covered by rebates after the assessment credit.

faq.q: Every winter we get huge icicles — roof problem or insulation problem?
faq.a: Almost always an attic problem: warm indoor air leaking up, melting snow that refreezes at the cold eaves. The audit's thermal scan finds the exact bypasses; sealing them plus a top-up beats heat cables every time.

faq.q: What does an audit cost in London?
faq.a: Typical Ontario pricing applies — roughly $400–$700 initial and $200–$400 follow-up — and the $600 HRSP rebate covers most of it when you complete the assessment path.

neighbourhoods.name: Oakridge
neighbourhoods.profile: West-end ranches and bungalows from London's post-war expansion: thin original batts, attics that started at R-10, and bare basements now being finished. The classic Oakridge audit finds an attic top-up and rim-joist sealing paying back faster than anything else — and flags aluminum wiring in the later builds before insulation work.

neighbourhoods.name: Masonville
neighbourhoods.profile: North London two-storeys from the poly-vapour-barrier era around the mall and university lands: nominal insulation is decent, so audits here chase comfort instead — unbalanced ducts, bonus rooms over garages, and ventilation that lags the airtightness. Duct testing is the add-on to request by name in Masonville.

neighbourhoods.name: Sunningdale
neighbourhoods.profile: London's newer executive stock at the city's north edge: code-era envelopes with big volumes to condition. Sunningdale audits are optimization audits — verifying the builder delivered the insulation you paid for, balancing long duct runs, sizing the eventual heat-pump swap with a proper F280 calculation, and assessing newer roofs for the solar + battery rebate.

neighbourhoods.name: Old North & Wortley Village
neighbourhoods.profile: London's yellow-brick century neighbourhoods. Solid-brick and balloon-frame construction means the thermal scan decides the wall strategy — and blower-door numbers here routinely reorder the whole renovation plan toward air sealing, attic, and basement first. Knob-and-tube and vermiculite checks come standard before any insulation work.

neighbourhoods.name: Byron
neighbourhoods.profile: Southwest ranches and side-splits toward the ski hill and ravine lots: split-levels leak at their many wall-roof junctions, and the neighbourhood's mature-tree shading changes the solar math. Air sealing plus attic work is the reliable Byron pairing, with ice-dam diagnostics in snowy winters.

neighbourhoods.name: White Oaks & Westminster
neighbourhoods.profile: South London's townhome and starter-home stock, including significant rental holdings: cheap, fast envelope wins — attic top-ups, weatherstripping, rim joists — that show up directly on utility-included operating costs. Landlords here can run the HRSP assessment path across multiple qualifying upgrades.

title: The Barrie & Simcoe County home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Barrie, Collingwood, Wasaga Beach and Simcoe County: snow-belt priorities, cottage conversions, HRSP rebates, and the region's registered advisors.
intro: Simcoe County homes fight real winter — lake-effect snow off Georgian Bay, design temperatures colder than the GTA's, and a housing stock that includes thousands of cottages promoted to year-round homes without year-round envelopes.
housingStock: Barrie's growth rings run 1970s to brand-new, with the older core sharing the usual thin-attic, leaky-rim profile. The distinctive regional stock is the converted cottage — Wasaga, Innisfil, Oro-Medonte — built for July and now heating through January: minimal wall insulation, vented crawlspaces, electric baseboard or propane. Collingwood adds ski-country chalets with cathedral ceilings that leak heat spectacularly.
commonFindings: Cottage conversions losing heat through uninsulated floors over crawlspaces
Cathedral ceilings with no realistic insulation path except during re-roofing — timing matters
Electric baseboard and propane heating with province-leading heat-pump paybacks
Snow-belt ice damming from attic bypasses
Wind-driven leakage on exposed lake-effect sites
programAngle: The Environment Network serves Simcoe County as the community organization alongside province-wide providers. Home Renovation Savings applies fully, and the region's electric- and propane-heated stock makes the up-to-$12,000 heat pump rebate the headline: converted cottages routinely cut heating costs 40%+ with a properly sized cold-climate unit.

faq.q: We winterized a cottage in Innisfil — where do we start?
faq.a: With the blower door: converted cottages leak in places house-brains don't think of (floor systems, crawlspace hatches, knee walls). Sealing plus floor/crawlspace insulation usually beats wall work, and the audit sequences it before you buy a bigger furnace you won't need.

faq.q: Do heat pumps handle Collingwood-area winters?
faq.a: Cold-climate units sized from a real heat-loss calculation do — the area's failures are almost all sizing and installation failures. Insist on the CSA F280 calc; it's the difference between a success story and a Facebook complaint.

title: The Peterborough & Kawarthas home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Peterborough and the Kawarthas: century homes, cottage-country conversions, GreenUP's long-running program, and the HRSP rebate stack.
intro: Peterborough has run community energy programs longer than almost anywhere in Ontario — GreenUP has been evaluating local homes for decades — and the region's mix of century town stock and lake-country conversions keeps its auditors busy.
housingStock: The city core holds solid century homes — brick and frame — with the usual empty walls and original attics, while East City and the avenues add early-1900s workers' housing. Outside town, the Kawarthas contribute cottage conversions on Chemong, Stoney, and the Otonabee: seasonal envelopes now heating year-round, often on propane or electric baseboard. Rural properties add oil furnaces and wood-stove hybrids to the diagnostic mix.
commonFindings: Century-home leakage and knob-and-tube flags in the city core
Cottage conversions with uninsulated floor systems and crawlspaces
Propane and baseboard heating primed for heat-pump conversion math
Wood-heat hybrid homes needing combustion-safety checks before tightening
Thin attics across every era — the region's default first fix
programAngle: GreenUP anchors the local audit supply alongside province-wide providers, and Home Renovation Savings covers the standard stack. For lake-country conversions on propane or baseboard, the heat pump rebate (up to $12,000) plus a proper heat-loss calculation is the region's highest-value combination.

faq.q: We heat partly with wood — does that complicate an audit?
faq.a: It makes one part more important: the combustion safety and spillage check. Tightening a house changes how stoves and chimneys draft, so the audit verifies venting before air-sealing work — a safety step, not paperwork.

faq.q: Who does audits in Peterborough?
faq.a: GreenUP is the community non-profit with decades of local evaluations; The Energuy covers the region commercially. Both are NRCan-licensed service organizations.

title: The Kingston & Eastern Ontario home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in Kingston: limestone heritage homes, post-war stock, student rentals, and the HRSP rebates — plus the registered advisors serving eastern Ontario.
intro: Kingston's limestone heritage is beautiful and thermally brutal: solid stone walls can't be cavity-filled, which makes measurement — not guesswork — the difference between a transformed old home and an expensive disappointment.
housingStock: The historic core runs to limestone and early brick — solid walls, stone foundations, heritage constraints on exterior changes. Around it: post-war bungalows toward the west end, 1970s splits, a large student-rental stock near Queen's with famously leaky envelopes, and rural properties on oil east and north of the city. Lake Ontario wind exposure makes air sealing punch above its weight.
commonFindings: Solid limestone walls where interior insulation strategy and moisture care must be designed, not improvised
Stone foundations needing moisture management before any basement insulation
Student rentals with the city's worst leakage numbers and cheapest fixes
Rural oil-heated homes with province-leading conversion paybacks
Heritage-district homes where invisible fixes (attic, basement, sealing) do the heavy lifting
programAngle: Home Renovation Savings applies normally, and heritage owners should note the rebate stack favours exactly the work heritage rules allow: air sealing, attic insulation, basement work, and mechanical upgrades — all invisible from the street. The audit documents pre-retrofit conditions, which some heritage processes ask for anyway.

faq.q: Can anything be done about solid limestone walls?
faq.a: Yes, but carefully: interior insulation on stone must manage moisture or it creates problems. That's why Kingston homes start with the audit — usually the attic, basement, and airtightness work delivers most of the win without touching the stone at all.

faq.q: I own a student rental — is an audit worth it?
faq.a: The leakage findings in Kingston's rental stock are routinely dramatic, the fixes cheap, and the assessment path rebates apply to landlords' properties. Lower bills also show up directly in utility-included rent margins.

title: The Niagara Region home energy guide
metaDescription: Home energy audits in St. Catharines, Niagara Falls, and Welland: post-war stock, milder-but-humid climate, HRSP rebates, and the registered advisors serving the peninsula.
intro: Niagara's climate is Ontario's mildest — which tempts homeowners to skip envelope work. The audits say otherwise: the peninsula's aging post-war stock leaks like anywhere else, and its humidity adds a moisture dimension most of the province doesn't fight.
housingStock: St. Catharines, Niagara Falls, and Welland are dominated by 1940s–70s bungalows and storey-and-a-halfs built through the canal-and-industry boom: thin walls, R-10 attics, damp basements. Older cores add pre-war brick, while wine-country and lakeshore infill brings newer stock. The region's humidity — lake on two sides — makes basement moisture and ventilation questions a standard part of local audits.
commonFindings: Damp basements where moisture strategy must precede insulation
R-10 attics across the post-war stock — the region's default first fix
Storey-and-a-half knee-wall spaces leaking heat in both directions
Humidity-driven condensation misread as window failure
Mid-century wiring and vermiculite flags in the older cores
programAngle: Green Venture's territory extends into Niagara alongside province-wide providers, and Home Renovation Savings runs the standard stack. The milder climate stretches heat-pump performance even further here — units rarely touch their cold-weather limits — making the up-to-$12,000 rebate an easy case when equipment comes due.

faq.q: Our basement smells musty — insulation or moisture problem?
faq.a: In Niagara, assume moisture first: the audit checks grading, drainage signals, and humidity before recommending insulation, because insulating a damp basement wall creates a mold farm. Order of operations is the whole game.

faq.q: Is a heat pump overkill for Niagara's mild winters?
faq.a: The opposite — mild winters are where heat pumps shine brightest, running at their most efficient range nearly all season. If your AC or furnace is near end-of-life, the rebate math is very friendly here.
